fixes.explanation: Light is a good guess, friend. But here the writer says the LORD "…has clothed and armed Himself with strength." (Psalm 93:1) The verse also says He is robed in majesty. Strength is the word the writer picks for this one.

Seen? I squint at my oven window all day, friend, but the writer isn't talking about eyesight. He says the world "…is firmly established; it cannot be moved." (Psalm 93:1) The point is how firmly it stands, so the word is moved.
True, friend. The writer says to the LORD, "Your throne was established long ago…" (Psalm 93:2) Verse 1 talked about Him, and now the writer says "Your." That's worth noticing.

Right on, friend. The writer tells the LORD, "You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) That's not just old. It's far bigger than anything I can compare it to, and I'm only a cookie stamper with a mustache.

Noah is a long way back, so I see the pull. But the writer tells the LORD, "You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) That goes back further than any person's days. Noah's days are way too recent for this verse.

Moses, the man God sent to bring Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), is a great name to land on, friend. But the writer tells the LORD, "You are from all eternity." (Psalm 93:2) That reaches back past Moses and past everyone else. The verse leaves no starting line at all.

Nations is a fair guess when something is rising, friend. But in this verse the writer says, "The floodwaters have risen, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:3) The rivers and seas are the ones making noise here. So the word is floodwaters.

Yes, friend. The writer says, "Above the roar of many waters—the mighty breakers of the sea—the LORD on high is majestic." (Psalm 93:4) The loudest thing in the verse is the sea, and the writer still puts the LORD above it. I can't even out-shout my own oven timer.

The whirlwind is a place the LORD speaks from in Job 38:1, so I see why you picked it. But this psalm is about water, and it says, "Above the roar of many waters—the mighty breakers of the sea—the LORD on high is majestic." (Psalm 93:4) So the answer is on high, above the roar. No wind needed here.

That's right, friend. The writer says, "holiness adorns Your house, O LORD…" (Psalm 93:5) Holiness is what the writer names as the house's adornment. My bakery gets sprinkles on the counter, and the writer names something better for His house.

Yes, baker. The writer says holiness adorns the LORD's house "…for all the days to come." (Psalm 93:5) That's no expiration date. My cookies can't say the same, because they go stale by the weekend. It's a lovely way to end the psalm.
